items.title: Armand Hug Interview, 1965-09-13
items.q: The interviewee does not mention Nick Garaka; the name is only introduced by the interviewer as an example of a 'rabid white musician' who complained about the glorification of older Negro musicians.

ctx.x: I think that the revival of Dixieland around Preservation Hall has been most fortunate for these musicians who hadn't played for so long. It gave them a chance to really get some work and it brought them out and some of them are real good musicians. However, I don't believe that this is just truly representative of just New Orleans musicians because you have so many musicians who played jazz, you know, I mean, Dixieland jazz and I believe a lot of people today hear Preservation Hall and they completely forget…

I think this brings to mind something else. It's kind of a confused tradition in New Orleans that's been brought up that the glorification of the older musicians by critics and by fans has often overemphasized the older Negro musicians. I think we had some rabid white musicians who'd complain about this like Nick Garaka in kind of extreme terms and it's been sort of a cluttered image that's been presented to the public. You as a person who understudied the earlier jazz musicians, colored and white, might be able…

Well, I'll put it the way Nick LaRocca put it, as you say. I think that the jazz music belongs to New Orleans. You hate to get into something where you say which was better, was the colored music better or the white jazz music better? I think that stuff stuff
